PaddySpeaks · Systems at the Whiteboard · Nº 44

The Private Health Lab Problem

Design a privacy-first health intelligence platform: Apple HealthKit, clinical data, local analytics and healthcare interoperability. The person keeps the data; the intelligence comes to them. Fifteen topics, eleven hard questions, the real code from a working local prototype, and the gate that real data must pass first.

LEVEL · Staff / Principal FIELD · Digital health · Privacy engineering READING · ~35 min DEMO · My Private Health Lab
DEPTH
Architecture15 topicsHard questionsCalculationsExercisesRubricReadiness gate

The senior move

Start from what exists: Apple sells no health-data or analytics service, and HealthKit is an on-device framework. Data reaches analysis only through the person, so put the analysis where the person is.

The architecture

Three modes with three trust boundaries: synthetic demo, local-first processing on the person’s device, and a managed service that is designed but not launched until a gate is passed.

The privacy model

Separate identity boundaries: the longitudinal record (identified, private), the provider handoff (identified, minimum necessary), cohort statistics (no identity, suppressed, noised).

The trap

“We’ll pull it from Apple’s API.” “Hashing the name makes it anonymous.” “Encrypted, therefore HIPAA-compliant.” “The model will find the trends.”
The interviewer

“People already own years of health data: Apple Health, a blood-pressure cuff, a scale, lab results and medication records from their clinics. Design a platform that turns it into understandable, traceable intelligence, without asking them to surrender it. Tell me what you would build first, what you would never build, and what has to be true before a single real record is processed.”

60 minuteswhiteboard + one coding exercisefollow-ups at every topic

The working answer: My Private Health Lab →Import & Privacy →Can it be anonymous? → The private lab reads synthetic Apple Health exports, device CSVs and FHIR bundles inside the browser tab; a browser test proves it makes no network request after a file is chosen. Its predecessor, Nº 43 The Health Intelligence Problem, designs the hosted pipeline.

ARCHITECTUREThree modes, three trust boundaries

Draw the boundary first, then the boxes. Where the data is processed decides who can see it, what can leak, and which laws apply.

ModeWhere data is processedWho can see itStatus
1 · Explore the demoPre-computed from synthetic seedsEveryone; nobody is realLive: /health-lab/
2 · My Private Health LabThe person’s browser, in a worker, in memoryThe person (and anything that controls their device or browser)Prototype; synthetic files only on the public site until the gate below
3 · Managed serviceA hosted service, after explicit consentThe service operator under contract, audit and lawDesigned, not built
Future · Companion appOn the iPhone, through HealthKit permissionsThe person; the developer only what the app sendsFeasibility design (Topic 3)

Mode 3, before upload, must show: what will be uploaded, why, where it is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, whether it is used for research or AI training (default: never), how to export and delete it, and which law applies.

FIFTEEN TOPICSWhat a strong candidate covers

Each topic: the question the interviewer asks, what a strong answer contains, the trap, and where the lab shows it.

1 · Product requirements

Ask: who is the user, what decision do they make, and what is the cost of a wrong answer? A person preparing for a visit, not a clinician on call. Five questions: what changed, what evidence supports it, what is missing, what deserves attention, what to discuss with a clinician.

Trap: starting with ingestion throughput. The five questions →

2 · Source-system feasibility

Apple offers no paid health-data API and does not sell analysis of a person’s data as a subscription; a reported AI health-coaching service was reportedly scaled back in February 2026. What exists: the Health app’s export (export.zip with export.xml, export_cda.xml, ECG CSVs, workout-route GPX), HealthKit for apps on the device, Health Records (FHIR) with a special entitlement, and certified US EHR patient APIs (SMART on FHIR).

Trap: designing around an Apple API that does not exist. Feasibility table with sources →

3 · Apple HealthKit integration

A native companion app requests read access type by type; the person can deny any type and the app cannot tell a denial from no data. New samples arrive through an observer query with background delivery; changes are fetched incrementally with an anchored query and a persisted anchor. Clinical records need the clinical-records entitlement and are read-only. App Store rules forbid using health data for advertising or data mining and keep personal health information out of iCloud documents.

Trap: “we’ll sync everything to our cloud nightly” without saying why each type is needed.

4 · Local versus cloud architecture

Local-first removes the largest breach target and most compliance surface, but loses cross-device history, server-side updates to rules, and support visibility. Cloud gives continuity and heavier analytics at the price of custody. The design decision is per purpose, not per company: trends locally; a provider handoff as an explicit, minimal, revocable transfer; cohort statistics only as aggregates.

Trap: calling local processing “perfectly anonymous” or “unconditionally secure”: the device, its extensions and its other apps remain risks.

5 · Secure data ingestion

Exports can be gigabytes: stream, never load. Read the ZIP’s central directory from the end, inflate the one entry with DecompressionStream, decode incrementally, tokenize records without building a DOM. Validate per record and keep going: a malformed date rejects one record, not the import. Cancel at any time; terminate the worker to delete.

Trap: DOMParser on a 2 GB file, or “upload it and we’ll parse server-side”. Exercise 1 →

6 · Canonical healthcare data models

One observation shape: code, value, canonical unit, original value and unit, instant, recorded offset, local date, source, device, method, kind (measured, estimated, external device, clinician-verified, patient-reported). FHIR at the edges (Observation, Condition, MedicationStatement/Request/Dispense), LOINC only where the mapping is certain, exact unit factors only.

Trap: storing FHIR JSON as the internal model, or treating a patient report as a clinical fact.

7 · Longitudinal analytics

Compare a person with their own baseline: windows (90 days against the previous 90), medians and ranges, coverage per window, persistence rules. Say “insufficient evidence” when coverage is too low. Coverage is computed before any finding:

{{COV_C}}
Carmen (synthetic)StatusEvidence

Rule: no measurement → no usable evidence → no conclusion. Coverage panel →

8 · Clinical safety boundaries

Typed signals, each with its rule and limits: baseline change, persistent trend, records that disagree, missing or stale data, a notification from a validated device feature, a reported symptom. Symptoms outrank metrics. No diagnosis, no prediction, no medication advice, no “you are fine”. A device notification is shown as the device’s own output with its documented limits, never re-interpreted.

Trap: a risk score. Signals for Dorothy →

9 · Privacy-preserving cohort analysis

Five kinds of comparison, never mixed: your earlier self, a validated clinical reference, a published study, a synthetic cohort, or none. In the demo, {{SUPPRESSED}} of {{STRATA}} synthetic strata have fewer than {{MIN_CELL}} people and are suppressed; {{MIN_CELL}} is a product setting, not a legal threshold. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise when statistics are published repeatedly, and its budget must be managed.

Trap: inventing a “legally sufficient” cell size. Cohort Explorer →

10 · Gen AI integration

Deterministic findings first; a model may only phrase facts that were computed, and every number in its answer must appear in a cited fact or the answer is withheld. Placement options: on-device model (most private, least capable), a managed model under contract with no retention and no training, or a general cloud API (never with raw files, never by default). Questions about diagnosis, medicines, safety or prediction are refused before any data is read.

Trap: “send the export to the model and ask what’s wrong”.

11 · Provider interoperability

Choose → Preview → Authorize → Deliver → Confirm. The clinician receives a one-page summary with sources and limits, and optionally a FHIR payload tagged patient-generated: medians and ranges, not every reading. Sharing is not monitoring: every summary says “not monitored”. Revocation stops future sharing; a copy the clinic filed stays under the clinic’s rules.

Trap: implying someone reviews data between visits. Provider Connect →

12 · Insurance commercialization

Four models: the person pays (subscription), a provider uses it in care, an employer or insurer subsidizes it for program results, or research with consent. A subsidizer receives program outcomes (enrolled, completed, validated measure changed), never raw streams; contracts forbid underwriting; data shared for care is unreachable from program pipelines. Never assume savings: model them as the payer’s hypothesis.

Trap: selling profiles or hidden derived risk scores. Economics →

13 · Scaling and cost modeling

Local-first has almost no marginal compute cost; fixed costs (security review, privacy review, support) dominate. A managed service adds storage, compute, model calls, security operations and compliance, and carries the breach risk. See the calculator below.

14 · Failure scenarios

A malformed export; a ZIP64 export the browser reader cannot handle (say so, do not crash); a duplicate re-import; a medication the record calls active that the person stopped; a lab two years old shown as current; a cohort cell that would identify one person; a browser extension that reads the page; a stolen laptop with a saved summary; a model that states a number that is not in the data.

15 · Regulatory and ethical trade-offs

Which law applies depends on who holds the data and why. HIPAA binds covered entities and their business associates, not a consumer app the person uses on their own; the FTC’s Health Breach Notification Rule covers many apps outside HIPAA; state laws such as Washington’s My Health My Data Act require consent to collect and to share consumer health data; in the EU and UK, health data is a special category under GDPR Article 9. Medical-device rules depend on the claims made. Ethically: the person must benefit from every use of their data.

Trap: “HIPAA-compliant because we use HTTPS and encryption.”

CALCULATIONSBack of the envelope, on your assumptions

Will a large export fit in a browser tab?

Every input is your assumption. The streaming reader holds one chunk at a time; what grows is the in-memory index of kept observations.

Differential privacy: the noise you pay for privacy

For a count with sensitivity 1, Laplace noise has scale 1/ε and 95% of releases fall within ±ln(20)/ε of the true value. Answering k queries spends k·ε under simple composition.

CODING EXERCISESThe real code, not a sketch

Exercise 1 · Stream one file out of a multi-gigabyte ZIP in a browser

Without a library and without reading the whole file into memory, find export.xml in an Apple Health ZIP and return a stream of its text. Discuss: why read from the end, what ZIP64 changes, how cancellation works, and what you do with a malformed record half-way through.

Reference solution (health-lab/engine.js)
{{ZIP_JS}}

Proven by node health-lab/tests/engine.mjs: the browser engine matches the Python pipeline on {{PARITY_FILES}} sample bundles, refuses an unmarked file, and rejects on cancel.

Exercise 2 · Reconcile a medication list across sources

You have a medication list entry, a prescription, pharmacy fills and the person’s own report. Produce one row per medicine with a status that never guesses: active, historical, discontinued or needs review. Never let a patient report overwrite the record, never let an old prescription make a medicine current, and never advise.

Reference solution (healthlab/ingest.py)
{{RECONCILE_PY}}

Exercise 3 · Whiteboard: a k-anonymity check before release

Given rows and a list of quasi-identifiers, return the share of rows in groups smaller than k, and the generalization (age band, region) that brings it to zero with the least information lost. Discuss why k-anonymity does not protect against attribute disclosure when everyone in a group shares the same diagnosis. The lab’s version is healthlab/anonymity.py.

REAL-DATA READINESS GATEWhat must be true before anyone’s real health data is processed

The public site accepts synthetic files only. Each item below needs an owner and evidence; none is claimed done until it is.

For local processing (Mode 2) on the public site

  • Independent security review of the private page, worker and engine, including the Content-Security-Policy and supply chain (no third-party scripts, pinned dependencies).
  • Served with HTTP security headers (CSP, frame-ancestors none, no referrer) from the host, not only a meta tag.
  • Automated test, in CI, that no request leaves the page after a file is chosen (exists: health-lab/tests/browser.mjs).
  • Privacy notice reviewed by counsel for the jurisdictions served; plain-language statement of what stays on the device and what the device itself can still expose.
  • Fuzzing of the parsers on malformed, truncated and hostile files; size limits; ZIP64 handled or refused clearly.
  • Accessibility review and a usability test with people who are not engineers.
  • Clinical review of every signal’s wording and limits.
  • An incident process: who is told, how fast, how the feature is switched off.

Additionally, for a managed service (Mode 3)

  • Determination of which laws apply (HIPAA role, FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, state consumer-health laws, GDPR) and the contracts they require.
  • Consent and disclosure screens tested for comprehension; separate consents for collection, sharing, research and AI.
  • Encryption with per-person keys; deletion by key destruction; retention schedule; tested restore.
  • Access control with least privilege, break-glass, and an audit log the person can see.
  • Penetration test and threat model refreshed; vendor and model-provider contracts with no retention and no training.
  • Clinical validation for any feature that could be read as a medical claim, and a regulatory analysis of device status.

Don’t ask people to surrender their data to gain intelligence. Design intelligence that respects their ownership of the data.— The design principle

One more thing… The next breakthrough in personal healthcare may not require a new sensor. It may require finally making sense of the information we already have.
